source_packet.title: Beyond the Pyramid: Bloom’s Taxonomy Meets Generative AI
source_packet.display_headline: Why AI-made assignments may hide learning
source_packet.evidence_scope: Selected source passages, not the complete article. Missing excerpt details do not prove absence in the original.
source_packet.evidence:
interpretation: GenAI has not simply added one more tool to the educator's kit; it has unsettled the very hierarchies that underwrote models like Bloom's Taxonomy. By revising, inverting, or 'UnBlooming' those models, the approaches in this article argue for designs that foreground recursion, reflection, and metacognitive growth as the real work of learning, especially in an age where GenAI is marketed as doing the 'thinking' for us. The future of learning is not arriving later. It is already here, unevenly distributed across classrooms, disciplines, and institutions. The educators who will shape that future are those willing to revise their most cherished frameworks, revisit their assessment practices, and keep asking questions about the kinds of thinkers, makers, and citizens we want our students to become.
explain: This article examines how several pre-AI frameworks no longer adequately account for this shift.

source_packet.title: The epistemic limits of generative AI disclosure in scholarly authorship
source_packet.display_headline: When AI disclosure redirects reader attention
source_packet.evidence_scope: Selected source passages, not the complete article. Missing excerpt details do not prove absence in the original.
source_packet.evidence:
interpretation: Generative AI disclosure should not be treated as a transparent reconstruction of manuscript production. Authors may accurately report particular operations, retained outputs, and verification procedures, but functional descriptions such as language polishing, structural editing, or idea generation remain retrospective classifications whose causal significance may not be fully recoverable. The distinction between observable actions, interpreted functions, and intellectual contributions places limits on what disclosure can establish, even when authors report their practices sincerely and in considerable detail. These limits matter because provenance information can influence scholarly evaluation. The readerly distraction model developed here distinguishes justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently connected to the disclosed operation or its plausible epistemic consequences.
explain: To examine this asymmetry, the article develops the readerly distraction model, distinguishing justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently related to the disclosed operation.

draft.deck: How does generative AI challenge traditional educational frameworks, and what are the limitations of disclosing its use in scholarly authorship?
draft.letter: In the age of generative AI, traditional educational frameworks like Bloom's Taxonomy are being challenged. Tina Austin and colleagues argue that AI requires new learning approaches, focusing on recursion, reflection, and metacognitive growth. Meanwhile, Minoru Matsui highlights the limitations of disclosing AI use in scholarly authorship, noting that while authors can accurately report their practices, the causal significance of these actions may not be fully recoverable. How do these challenges and limitations interplay in shaping the future of education and scholarly practices?

Tina Austin and colleagues: Tina Austin and colleagues discuss how generative AI challenges traditional educational frameworks, emphasizing the need for new approaches that focus on recursion, reflection, and metacognitive growth.

Minoru Matsui: Minoru Matsui explores the limitations of generative AI disclosure in scholarly authorship, noting that while authors can accurately report their practices, the causal significance of these actions may not be fully recoverable.

Do the challenges posed by generative AI to traditional educational frameworks exacerbate or mitigate the limitations of disclosing its use in scholarly authorship, and how might this affect the future of education and scholarly practices?

Minoru Matsui: The article explores the limitations of generative AI disclosure in scholarly authorship, noting that while authors can accurately report their practices, the causal significance of these actions may not be fully recoverable. It introduces the readerly distraction model to address the issue of disproportionate attention to features that are not directly related to the disclosed operation.

How does generative AI challenge traditional educational frameworks, and what are the limitations of disclosing its use in scholarly authorship?
